name: Slagside Scrapper's Half-Plate
description: Built for the reclaimed industrial zones where the Gray Zone bleeds into active demolition corridors — places where falling debris, chemical runoff, and territorial disputes are all equally lethal. The foundation is a long-sleeve shirt in thick faded black synthetic, the kind of fabric that starts stiff and softens over years of wear; this one is soft. Over it, a sleeveless work jacket in rust-orange canvas has been armored with salvaged panel sections: the left shoulder carries a curved piece of hard composite cut from what was clearly once a vehicle door interior, strapped in place with three-point industrial webbing. The right shoulder is open — a deliberate choice, the straps there cut away to accommodate a chrome arm prosthetic that extends from just below the shoulder, matte-finished with the manufacturer's markings ground off, fingers worn smooth at the tips from use. The jacket's front is asymmetrically buttoned, the left side carrying six functioning cargo pockets, the right kept clear for arm movement. Trousers are combat-cut in worn olive, the thighs and shins reinforced with segments of rubber conveyor belt stitched over the original fabric, the knees blown out and repaired with self-repair tape that has yellowed and is beginning to peel at one edge. A thick belt in cracked brown synthetic leather carries a multi-tool in a molded holster, a small medical kit in a battered tin, and two more pockets whose contents make rectangular outlines under the flap. Boots are mid-calf, steel-reinforced at the toe, the right boot modified with a wider toe box to accommodate what looks like the beginning of a toe-chrome situation — a single augmented toe visible at the boot's open vamp when the laces are loose. A dented matte-black hard hat hangs from the belt by a clip, not worn, just carried.
materials: mid-calf steel-toe boots with modified vamp
functionality: Composite shoulder armor provides impact and shrapnel resistance on the dominant-side. Chrome arm prosthetic is fully functional with ground-off identifying marks (unregistered aug). Rubber-reinforced trouser panels protect against abrasion and minor chemical splash. Belt system distributes essential tools and medical supplies across the waist for fast access. Steel-toe boots protect against falling debris. Wide-vamp right boot accommodates partial toe augmentation without restricting movement. Hard hat carried rather than worn signals the wearer moves between active and passive hazard zones frequently.
what_it_says: This person works the demolition corridors and scrap fields, probably without a permit. The unregistered chrome arm says they can't afford authorized aug maintenance and don't want to be tracked by the corponation that made it. The asymmetry of the jacket — armored left, open right — is a practical adaptation that also reads as a signature. The dented hard hat on the belt rather than the head is a the Gray Zone joke: I know the rules, I just choose when to follow them.
worn_by: the Gray Zone salvage crew members
unregistered aug users who work physical labor
territorial enforcers in industrial the Gray Zone zones
manufacturer: Self-assembled; jacket is unmarked factory seconds; armor panel is cut salvage; chrome arm is black-market aug of unknown origin with identifying marks removed
price_range: Φ25–Φ60 for clothing components; chrome arm separately valued at Φ300–Φ800 on the black market
story_hooks: The chrome arm's identifying marks were ground off, but a corponation security division has a new scanning protocol that reads sub-surface serial numbers — and this arm just pinged in a system the wearer didn't know existed.
The salvage crew this person works with found something in a demolition site that they weren't supposed to find, and now someone is trying to determine exactly who was on the crew that day.

The dented hard hat has a sticker on the inside brim — a the Gray Zone gang territorial mark that the wearer may not even know is there, left by a previous owner, now creating a case of mistaken affiliation.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist street-salvage silhouette — asymmetrical and purposefully unbalanced, built from reclaimed industrial materials. The figure reads as a functional survivor: one chrome arm catching light against faded black, rust-orange canvas vest over weathered synthetic base, olive combat trousers patched with conveyor belt rubber. The hard hat hanging from the belt like a tool rather than protective wear signals someone operating in zones where safety equipment is aspirational. The overall impression is raw, capable, and unmarked by any official brand — pure sub-grade engineering.
physical_description.fit: Intentionally loose and mobile — the jacket's sleeveless cut accommodates the chrome prosthetic; asymmetrical button placement leaves the right side clear for arm access and movement; combat trousers are cut wide through the hip and thigh for climbing and crouching, with reinforced panels that don't flex. Everything is built for function, not flattery. Compression in the core from the heavy belt rig; mobility prioritized everywhere else.
physical_description.primary_material: Base: thick faded black synthetic-wool blend, soft from years of industrial wear. Work jacket in salvaged rust-orange canvas. Armor panel: hard composite salvage (vehicle origin). Trousers: worn olive cotton/synthetic blend with rubber conveyor belt reinforcement. Belt: cracked brown synthetic leather. Chrome arm: matte-finished black-market prosthetic, markings removed.
physical_description.texture: Varied and tactile — the black synthetic base is soft and worn smooth; the orange canvas is stiff with industrial residue; the composite armor panel is hard and slightly weathered with micro-scratches; rubber reinforcements are grippy and show cracking at stress points; the belt is cracked and aged. The chrome arm is satin-smooth in finish, fingers worn to a dull sheen from use. Seams are heavy-gauge, visible, and reinforced.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant: matte black (synthetic base, hard hat, chrome arm finish). Rust-orange canvas work jacket. Weathered olive trousers. Cracked brown belt. Yellowed self-repair tape at the knee patches. Dull metallic accents from the chrome prosthetic and belt hardware.
physical_description.closures: Asymmetrical button front (left side only, six buttons); heavy industrial webbing straps (three-point at left shoulder armor); boots with standard lacing, loose fit; belt buckle in scuffed matte metal; molded holster and tin pouches on belt rig.
distinctive_features: Left shoulder: curved composite armor panel strapped with three-point industrial webbing, clearly salvaged from a vehicle
Right shoulder: open for chrome prosthetic arm integration; original straps cut away
Asymmetric cargo pockets (six on left, none on right for arm clearance)
Thigh and shin reinforcements: segments of stitched-on conveyor belt rubber over original fabric
Knee damage: intentional rips repaired with yellowing self-repair tape, peeling at edges
Right boot: modified wider toe box, augmented toe visible when laces are loose (early-stage toe-chrome)
Belt rig: multi-tool in molded holster, battered medical kit tin, two mystery rectangular pouches
Hard hat: matte black, dented, hung from belt clip rather than worn — tool, not gear
No manufacturer markings, no corporate branding, no identifying details
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 salvage — unmistakable sub-grade assembly. Every piece is reclaimed, salvaged, or black-market. The patchwork construction, removed identifying marks, and functional rather than stylish design signal someone operating outside regulated zones.
physical_description.cultural_context: Slagside Scrapper. Someone who works active demolition corridors, reclaimed industrial zones, and territorial dispute areas where the infrastructure is literally collapsing and being stripped. The outfit says: I repair what others abandon; I augment myself in the dark; I carry my own medical supplies because formal healthcare won't reach where I work; I don't have a safety net, so I build my own armor. The mixed chrome and salvage construction indicates either: long-term sub-grade survival, or deliberate choice to operate outside corpo regulatory spaces.
physical_description.condition_typical: Weathered and intentionally maintained. Nothing pristine, but nothing falling apart — yet. The self-repair tape at the knees is deteriorating, suggesting this outfit is at a tipping point: functional now, but with visible wear that suggests either replacement or deeper rebuilding soon. The yellow tape peeling is not negligence; it's a record of how long this person has been doing this work.
